newsitem.title: USA: Antimony supply to outstrip demand - Roskill.
newsitem.headline: Antimony supply to outstrip demand - Roskill.

text.p: Antimony prices could remain volatile for some time because of continued dependence on China, but rocketing tags are ruled out despite strong growth expected, analyst Mark Seddon of Roskill Information Services said.
Seddon expected antimony prices to hover between $2,500 and $3,500 a tonne over the next few years.
"The industry needs prices to be maintained at above $3,000 a tonne in order to ensure a stable supply of material," Seddon told Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals Seminar.
"A sustained period of prices below this level would put pressure on all producers and could lead to supply shortages and further price volatility."
Prices fell to a low of $2,000 a tonne in November last year and have firmed slightly in recent weeks, Seddon said.

China accounts for 70 percent of global antimony production, but the world's dependence on this country could be lessened if the clutch of projects in the Former Soviet Union come on stream, but they are dependent on foreign cash and need to increase dwindling ore reserves.

"Overall, a growth rate of between 3 and 4 percent to 2000 for primary antimony demand appears to be reasonable," Seddon said. "This would add a further 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes a year to current consumption of antimony by the end of the decade."
Although strong growth is forecast, there is enough capacity in the market to cope with this growth and there are plans for a potential 26,000 tonnes of new annual capacity.
Most existing producers are not running flat out.
Nevertheless, Roycefield Resources of Canada is planning to commission and integrated mine and antimony trioxide plant in Newfoundland in the first half of this year with a capacity of 6,500 tonnes.

And Suzuhiro of Japan has formed a joint venture to produce high purity antimony trioxide in Hunan Province China with output this year set at 1,200 tonnes, with capacity rising to 3,000 tonnes a year, Seddon noted.
"However, at current price levels, it is unlikely that companies will produce at anything near full capacity," Seddon said.
World mine production of antimony was 126,217 tonnes of contained metal in 1995, with 124,300 tonnes of refined metal capacity available.
Demand in 1995 for antimony trioxide was estimated at 75,000 tonnes.
Flame retardants in plastics, rubber, textiles, adhesives and paper are the leading consumer of antimony, followed by catalysts and metallurgical uses such as in lead for batteries.
Substitution of with cheaper materials does not take place until antimony prices reach $6,000 a tonne as it did in 1994, one delegate told the seminar.
